questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man with a 10-day history of fever, nausea and vomiting, and progressive confusion remains hospitalized because his symptoms have not resolved despite treatment with broad-spectrum antibiot ics. He has a 6-year history of severe emphysema treated with courses of corticosteroids during the past year. Medications include intravenous ceftriaxone and ampicil lin, albutero l inhalers, theophy lline, and prednisone. He is confused and stuporous. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows meningismus. An MRI of the brain shows diffuse meningeal enhancement with a basilar predominance. A lumbar puncture is done; cerebrosp inal fluid analysis shows a leukocyte count of 322/mm 3 (86% lymphocytes), a glucose concentration of 17 mg/dL, and a protein concentration of 212 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Chronic use of immunosuppressants including glucocorticoids increase the likelihood of tuberculosis reactivation. Tubercu lous meningitis typically presents with nuchal rigidity, fever, and altered mental status, similar to the symptoms seen in bacterial meningitis. However, unlike bacterial meningitis which presents acutely, tuberculous meningitis typica lly shows a subacute presentation. Presence of cranial nerve palsies is also more likely in tuberculous meningitis than bacterial meningitis. Physical examination may show a positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign, indicative of meningea l irritation. Results of laboratory studies will show nonspecific changes including leukocytosis and mild anemia. A tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay are usually positive, but a negative result is also possible. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will reveal an increased opening pressure, increased white blood cell count with prominent lymphocytes, increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration. Culture of the CSF for acid-fast bacilli may be positive, though the sensitivity of this test for tuberculous meningitis is less than 50%. Radiologic evaluation may show basilar exudates, as in this case, as well as periventricu lar infarcts and hydrocephalus.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Herpes simplex encephalitis (Choice A) presents with fever, altered mental status, and neurologic abnormalities, such as seizure, aphasia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve deficits. Neuroimaging will typically show changes in the temporal lobe. The basilar predominance in this case is more suggestive of a tuberculous meningitis than herpes encephalitis. Lyme disease (Choice B) caused by disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi infection may cause neuropathy and meningitis. However, this would be expected to be accompanied by a rash in the pattern of erythema migrans and history of tick exposure.

questionStem: An 8-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of increased irritability over the past month. During this period, she has had interm ittent low-grade fever and episodes of stiffening of her body. Her father reports that she previously interacted with them and smiled when prompted but has not made eye contact for the past 3 days. She has a history of hypotonia. She cannot yet roll over or sit up. Her parents are third cousins. She is awake and irritable and has poor visual regard. Exam ination of the skin shows no neurocu taneous lesions. The optic nerves are pale. Neurologic examination shows hyperex tension of the head and back, ankle spasticity, and fisting. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk, and Babinski sign is present. correctExplanation: This infant's presentation of fever, spasticity, hypotonia, vision loss, optic nerve pallor, and Babinski sign, as well as a family history of consanguinity are consistent with a diagnosis of Krabbe disease, also known as galactosylceramide lipidosis. Krabbe disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GALC gene that encodes galactocerebrosidase, the deficiency of which results in accumulation of galactocerebroside and demyelinating neuronal degeneration. Patients typically present within the first year of life with progressive neurologic degeneration, spasticity, stiffness, seizures, feeding difficulty, and peripheral neuropathy, including optic neuropathy. The diagnosis is confirmed with serum enzyme assays, although MRI of the brain will show white matter degeneration caused by demyelination. There is no effective treatment for Krabbe disease and most affected children die during the first several years of life.

Dandy-Walker malformation does not typically present with spasticity and stiffness and presents with papilledema rather than optic nerve pallor. questionStem: A 57-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after a simple partial seizure. Examination shows mild weakness of the right lower extremity. A CT scan of the head shows a 1.5-cm , uniformly and intensely enhancing parasagitta l mass in the left frontal region. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Meningioma is a common, benign centra l nervous system (CNS) tumor derived from the meninges that occurs along the surfaces of the brain and spina l cord, often in the parasagittal region. They occur in women more often than men and are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Patients may be asymptomatic or experience seizures or focal neurologic deficits related to the tumor location. Meningiomas are typically benign but can be malignant. Malignant meningiomas may grow rapidly, leading to symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (eg, postural headache, nausea, papilledema), or may metastasize. Meningiomas appear as well-circumscribed, extra-axia l (ie, outside of the brain parenchyma) masses that compress the parenchyma. They show uniform enhancement on imaging. Definitive diagnosis requires histologic examination of tissue, which will show spindle cells arranged in a whor led pattern with psammoma bodies. Treatment may include antiepileptics or surgical resection to alleviate the tumoral mass effect if significant, though often, periodic survei llance is all that is necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Astrocytoma (Choice A) is a primary CNS neoplasm that can occur as benign pilocytic astrocytoma in children or malignant glioblastoma multiforme (Choice C) in adults. Glioblastoma are highly malignant tumors appearing as intra-axial masses in the cerebral hemispheres, which typically show areas of necrosis and can spread to the opposite hemisphere across the corpus callosum. Ependymoma (Choice B) is a CNS neoplasm formed from ependymal cells. Location typical ly involves the fourth ventricle. Histologic characteristics include perivascular pseudorosettes formed by malignant cells arranged around a blood vessel. Schwannoma (Choice E) are benign tumors that arise from Schwann cells in peripheral nerve sheaths. They commonly affect the facial and vestibulococh lear nerves, and mass effect may result in sensorineural hearing loss or ataxia. They are associated with neurofibromatosis type 2. - - - - - - -- - - - . ' - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - ..

Hie immediately had the onset of pain in his neck and a sensation of an electric shock radiating from his neck to his left shoulder. He did not have loss of consciousness. He was able to stand , and two friends helped him out of the water i nto a supine position on the dock. Muscle strength is 3/5 on extension of the left wrist. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. Babinski sign is absent. questionStem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of headache and left-sided weakness that have become increasingly severe. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril and chronic neck pain treated with 325-mg aspirin. On arrival, he appears mildly lethargic. His pulse is 60/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate weakness of the lower left side of the face. Muscle tone is decreased in the left upper and lower extremities. Muscle strength is 4/5 on the left and 5/5 on the right. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ on the left. Babinski sign is present on the left. A CT scan of the head without contrast is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive intracerebra l hematomas (ICHs) can occur in patients with chronic hypertension, typically because of hemorrhage from small penetrating arteries in the pons, midbrain, thalamus, putamen, caudate, or cerebellum. Risk factors for hypertensive ICH include uncontrolled hypertension and antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, such as with aspirin or warfarin. Patients can present with headache, vomiting, confusion, altered mental status, stupor, or coma. Focal neurologic deficits depend on the site of the ICH and can include hemiparesis, hemisensory symptoms, gaze palsy, dysarthria, aphasia, or if in the cerebellum, ataxia, vomiting, and disequilibrium. Patients may manifest upper motoneuron examination findings such as spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar reflex (Babinski sign). Diagnosis is made with noncontrast CT scan of the head which will show hyperdense intraparenchyma l products, which is the appearance of acute bleeding in the brain as seen in this patient's right hemisphere. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause .... https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 6 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Clinical Neurology Self-Assessment
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (Choice A) occurs secondary to amyloid deposition in cerebral blood vessels and leptomeninges. It can cause spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage in older adults, typically in a lobar location, because of the location of amyloid deposits in cortical vessels. In contrast, hypertensive hemorrhages typically occur in a deep location such as the putamen, thalamus, midbrain, or pons. lschemic cerebral infarction (Choice C) can occur as a result of thromboembol ic occlusion of cerebral arteries. Patients typically present with acute focal neurologic deficits, especially on one side of the body, and may have speech difficulty, dysarthria, or aphasia. A CT scan would not show hyperdense blood products unless the infarction is complicated by hemorrhagic conversion. Ruptured arteriovenous malformation (Choice D) can lead to intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Arteriovenous malformations are uncommon and usually present in individuals younger than 50 years old with intracranial hemorrhage, seizure, neurologic deficit, or headache, or may be an incidental finding. In an older patient with uncontrolled hypertension, a hypertensive intracerebral hematoma is more likely. Ruptured berry aneurysm (Choice E) typically leads to a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Patients typically present with an acute, severe headache ( often described as the worst headache of the patient's life), along with neck stiffness, photophobia, and possible stupor or coma in severe cases. CT scan of the head typically shows hyperdense blood products in the cerebral sulci and basal cisterns. Educational Objective: Hypertensive intracerebral hematomas can occur in patients with chronic hypertension, typically as a result of hemorrhage from small penetrating arteries in the pons, midbrain, thalamus, putamen, caudate, or cerebellum. Patients can present with headache, vomiting, confusion, altered mental status, stupor, upper motoneuron signs, and focal neurologic deficits such as hemiparesis and hemisensory symptoms.

Initial ly, she had difficulty jumping; 2 weeks later she had a tingling feeling in the toes of her right foot that quickly spread to the left foot. Over the past 2 weeks, she has stumbled and fallen severa l times. Exam ination of the upper extremities shows normal findings. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the lower extremities. She is unable to heel walk and has mild difficulty walking on her toes and rising from a low squatting position. Positio n sensation is norma l, but pinprick feels less sharp distally and occasiona l light touch stimuli are missed over the toes . Peronea l motor conduction velocity is moderately slowed (22 m/sec; N=42-57). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctExplanation: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradicu lopathy (CIDP) is an immune-mediated demye linating condition affecting the spinal nerve roots. The pathogenesis of CIDP involves inflammation of myelin by an unknown mechanism. The ventra l nerve roots containing motor efferents are common ly involved, though the dorsa l nerve root (control ling sensation) may also be affected. As such, patients typical ly present with relapsing-remitting or gradual ly progressive symmetric muscle weakness with depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes (reflecting a lower motoneuron pattern of dysfunction) that affects the proxima l and dista l lower extremities simultaneous ly and may also affect the upper extremities. Autonomic dysfunction may occur but is typically mild. Sensory deficits may occur (though these symptoms are typica lly mild compared to motor dysfunction). A slowing of conduction velocity on nerve conduction studies indicates demyelination and supports the diagnosis. The diagnosis is further supported by increased cerebrospinal fluid protein with normal cell counts on lumbar puncture, termed albuminocyto logic dissociation and thought to reflect generalized inflammation. Management includes glucocorticoids, immunomodulators, plasma exchange, or intravenous immunog lobulin therapy.

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of progressive weakness of his legs during the past week. He has chronic kidney disease and receives dialysis three times weekly via a percutaneous tunneled catheter. Last week , he had an episode of sweating and chills. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, and blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg. Examination shows severe tenderness to percussion over the lumbar spine. The catheter site appears normal. There is trace edema of the lower extremities. Muscle strength is 3/5 on flexion and extension of the knees and ankles. Deep tendon reflexes are increased at the patellae. Most patients have a history of another preceding or associated (even occult) infection and often have a history of immunocompromise (eg, diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, alcohol use disorder). Epidural abscess is more common in patients with a history of intravenous drug use or indwelling intravenous lines. Infectious organisms usually spread to the epidural space hematogenously, from spinal surgery, or from adjacent osteomyelitis. Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent causative organism. Patients present with signs and symptoms of fever, altered mental status, meningismus, localized back pain, and tenderne ss to palpation, along with weakness, numbness, and paralysis below the affected spinal level as a result of cord compression. Treatment is with broad spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage of the abscess. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by his wife 30 minutes after a 15-minute episode of inability to speak. He has a 15-year history of poorly controlled hypertension . Three weeks ago, he had a transmural myocardial infarction and underwe nt placement of a stent in the left anterior descending coronary artery. Current medications include clopidogrel, benazepril, and 81-mg aspirin. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. On arrival, he is alert and oriented to person , place, and time. His pulse is 60/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. A grade 1 /6 systolic murmur is heard best at the second left intercostal space. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Carotid duplex ultrasonograp hy shows 40% stenosis of the left carotid artery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: An embolic ischemic stroke involves an event in which a clot breaks off and travels to the brain, occluding blood flow within a cerebra l artery. Emboli can originate from proxima l vessels, such as the internal carotid artery, or from an atrial or ventricular thrombus. This patient had a recent myocardial infarction, which predisposes him to a ventricular aneurysm. Ventricular aneurysms are more likely to form in the case of large, anterior myocardia l infarctions as a result of obstruction of the left anterior descending coronary artery, as was the case in this patient. A small systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation may be heard. Within the aneurysm, as a result of areas of stagnant blood flow and despite being on clopidogre l, a thrombus can form that can embolize and cause an ischemic stroke. If a patent foramen ovale is present, an embolism may arise from either the right or left side of the heart. This patient also has other risk factors for ischemic stroke including hypertension and atherosclerotic disease. Because his symptoms resolved within less than 24 hours, his embolic event is classified as a transient ischemic attack.

questionStem: One month after starting isoniazid and rifampin therapy for pulmonary tubercu losis, a 62-year-old woma n develops weakness, fatigue, and paresthesias. Examination shows pallor and diminished light touch sensation in the extremities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in 9 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 78 µm3 Leukocyte count 8000/mm3 Platelet count 210,000 /mm3 These symptoms are most likely to respond to treatment with which of the following?
correctExplanation: lsoniazid and rifampin are used in the treatmen t of primary tuberculosis, which results from an initial exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. lsoniaz id binds vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) which may result in early excretion and inactivation of pyridoxine, and also inhibits pyridoxine phosphokinase, which is necessary to activate it. Pyridoxine deficiency results, of which primary symptoms are peripheral neuropathy and paresthesia. Pyridox ine deficiency limits synthesis of histamine, hemoglobin, and neurotransm itters including epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin, and y-aminobutyric acid (GABA). In addition to peripheral neuropathy, deficiency common ly presents with dermatitis, siderob lastic anemia, glossitis, and seizures. These adverse effects may all be avoided by pyridoxine supplementation in all patients taking isoniazid.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Folic acid (Choice A) is converted to tetrahydrofo lic acid and is used as a coenzyme in the synthesis of nucleotides and nucleosides. Folate is contained in leafy vegetab les and absorbed in the jejun um. Folate deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcoholism, and patients taking anti-folate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). It is not caused by isoniazid or rifampin and is not responsible for this patient's symptoms. Iron (Choice B) deficiency also presents with microcytic anemia. However, it is not induced by isoniazid or rifampin and its supplementation in this case would not address the symptoms of pyridoxine deficiency.

questionStem: A 22-year-o ld man who is a collegiate volleyball player comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of progressive pain and weakness in his right shoulder. There is no history of trauma. He is 196 cm (6 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2. There is significant loss of muscle mass in the dorsal scapula region, especial ly in the area of the scapular spine. Passive abduction and externa l rotation of the right shoulder and protraction of the scapula reproduce the pain. There is weakness with resisted externa l rotation and initiation of abduction. Active range of motion shows full flexion and abduct ion. Sensory examinat ion shows no cutaneous deficits along the right side of the neck or in the right upper extremity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: The patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are most consistent with entrapment of the suprascapu lar nerve. The suprascapular nerve originates from the superior trunk of the brachia! plexus and innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. Nerve compression secondary to traction injury is common among volleyball players. Irritation of the suprascapular nerve results in pain along the course of the nerve and may result in chronic neuropathy with subsequent muscle wasting, atrophy, and degeneration of the infraspinatus and supraspinatus muscles. The supraspinatus is responsib le for adduction of the shoulder, and the infraspinatus is responsible for external rotation of the shoulder, which reproduce the pain and disclose weakness in this patient. Initial treatment is conservative with activity modification and physical therapy. Operative intervention may be required.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adhesive capsulitis (Choice A) is a common cause of shoulder pain in adults, characterized by severe ly limited range of motion. Patients typically note a gradua l onset of progressive shoulder stiffness and pain. Physical examination would disclose limited range of motion while this patient discloses full range of motion. Axillary nerve damage (Choice B) results in weakness of the deltoid and teres minor, which abduct and stabilize the shoulder. The axillary nerve gives rise to the superficial lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, and sensory deficits would be expected if injured. Brachia! plexus palsy (Choice C) describes a range of injury to the nervous system complex that gives rise to the nerves of the upper extremity. The mechanism is usually high-impact trauma or forced abduction of the shoulder. Physical examination typica lly discloses motor and sensory deficits involving several periphera l nerves.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician with her husba nd because of a 6-month history of fluctuating symptoms including fatigue, loss of balance, blurred vision, and the sensation of pins and needles over he r arms and legs. Her husband says that she has also had mood swings with episodes of uncontro llable crying over the past 2 months. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/86 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows reduced medial gaze of the left eye and numbness to pinprick over the left distal lower extremities. Rombe rg sign is present. Babinski sign is present on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalam in) concentration
choices.F: Measurement of urine porphob ilinogen concentration
choices.I: VDRL test in cereb rospinal fluid

correctExplanation: Multiple sclerosis (MS), the most prevalent immune-mediated demye linating disease, may present with episodic or progressive neurologic dysfunction. According to the McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis, patients must have evidence of demyelinating lesions that are separated in time and location. This evidence is typically based on subjective symptoms and radiologic studies. Lesions affecting the left medial longitudina l fasciculus (leading to decreased medial gaze of the left eye), the prefronta l cortex or corticobulbar tracts (leading to pseudobu lbar affect, or uncontrollable crying), and the major central nervous system (CNS) tracts innervating the extremities (lesions of the corticospina l tract causing Babinski sign, spinothalamic tract causing decreased pinprick, dorsal column-media l lemniscus causing Romberg sign and paresthesia) are likely separated in space. This patient experienced two discrete periods of symptom onset at 6 months and 2 months, illustrating separation in time. MRI typically shows white matter hyperintensities in the periventricular region, cortex, subcortical region, cerebel lum, or spine. Oligoclonal bands of immunog lobulins, indicating immune overactivation, can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid but are not necessary for diagnosis. Treatment includes corticosteroids for symptomatic management of acute flares and long-term disease-modifying treatments such as interferon or monoclonal antibodies.

questionStem: A physician makes a house call for an 87-year-old woman who is unable to come to the office because of difficulty with transportat ion. Her family reports that she has fallen frequent ly during the past 6 weeks. The patient says that she has had some difficulty feeling where her feet are but that she is otherwise well. She has not had loss of consciousness. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medicat ions. Vital signs are within normal limits. Muscle strength is 4/5 on flexion of the hips and extension of the knees and ankles bilaterally. Proprioceptio n and sensation to vibrat ion are decreased in the lower extrem ities. Sensation to light touch is intact. She has a slapping gait. Mental status examination shows no abnorma lities. The physician counsels the patient about making enhancements to her home to prevent falls. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Measurement of serum vitamin B12 (cobalamin) concentration
choices.C: X-rays of the lumbosacra l spine

correctExplanation: Subacute combined degeneration, caused by demyelination of the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts, is a feature of vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) deficiency. Subacute combined degeneration causes a combination of motor and sensory symptoms including ataxic gait, muscle weakness, paresthesia , and loss of proprioception and vibration sense. The effects of these features may include frequent falls, as in this case. Vitamin B 12 deficiency is often a result of inadequate dietary intake, seen in veganism, malabsorption, or pernicious anemia. Occasiona lly, elderly patients with poor nutrition may develop B 12 deficiency. Other manifestations include dementia and megaloblastic anemia. In an elderly patient with an acute or subacute change in behavior or activities of daily living, organic causes such as vitamin deficiency should be ruled out.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Determination of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Choice A) may be useful in suppo rting the diagnosis of an inflammatory process, such as polymyositis, as the cause of this patient's lower extremity weakness. However, erythrocyte sedimentation rate is nonspecific and would not suggest a definitive diagnosis. Furthermore, the patient's symptoms are more consisten t with vitamin B 12 deficiency than an inflammatory process. X-rays of the lumbosacral spine (Choice C) may be warranted in a patient with recent falls who is suspected to have fractures or other musculoskeletal pathology. However, it is not useful in diagnosing subacute combined degeneration. EEG (Choice D) is the test of choice in diagnosing a seizure disorder. questionStem: A 27-year-o ld nulligravid woman has had cafe au lait spots and multiple neurofibromas since birth. A diagnosis of neurofibromatos is is made. She is concerned that she might pass this condition on to her children. Her parents and three siblings do not have this disorder. The risk for neurofibromatosis in her children is closest to which of the following?

choices.A: 50% for each child , since neurofibromatosis is autosomal dominan t
choices.B: 25% for each child, since neurofibroma tosis is autosoma l recess ive
choices.C: 10% for each child, since neurofibroma tosis is contro lled by severa l genes
choices.D: No risk, since neurofibromatos is is not a genet ic disorde
choices.E: No risk, since the patient represe nts a new mutat ion

correctExplanation: Neurofibromatosis type I is a genetically inherited disorder caused by a defect in NF1, the gene which encodes neurofibromin on chromosome 17. It follows an autosoma l dominant pattern of inheritance. It is characterized by a constellation of cutaneous manifestations (eg, neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, cafe au lait spots, and axillary freckling), a variety of central nervous system tumors including optic nerve glioma and iris hamartoma (ie, Lisch nodu le), and bony abnorma lities such as long bone dysp lasia and sphenoid wing dysplasia. Patients are also at higher risk for developing astrocytomas, brainstem gliomas, and soft tissue sarcomas. Because it follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, only one alle le is needed to develop the condition. Thus, the chance of this patient passing on the dominant allele containing the mutation on chromosome 17 is 50% for each child.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. 25% for each child (Choice B) wou ld be the chance of a child deve loping an autosoma l recessive disease if both his or her parents were carriers. The defect in NF1 that causes neurofibromatosis type I is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. 10% for each child (Choice C) could be the chance of a deve loping a disease which is controlled by several genes, or for which there is variable penetrance or expressivity, but neurofibromatosis type I is caused by a defect in a single gene, NF1, located on chromosome 17. No risk for developing neurofibromatosis (Choice D) is incorrect as the disease is a genetic disorder. Whi le the patient likely does represent a new mutation (Choice E) given that her parents are unaffected, this does not change the patient's risk for passing on her mutation to her children. Educational Objective: Neurofibromatosis type I is a genetica lly inherited disorder caused by a defect in NF1, the gene which encodes neurofibromin on chromosome 17. It follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. The chance of an affected patient having an affected child is 50%.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician 2 hours after the sudden onset of visual loss in his right eye. He has no history of similar episodes . He has a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and hypertension treated with lisinopril. He sustained a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. His pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 170/96 mm Hg. Findings on right funduscopic exam ination are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting signs and symptoms of abrupt, painless vision loss and a pale fundus with normal fovea l color are consistent with a diagnosis of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). CRAO commonly occurs as a result of embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery but may occur secondary to vasculitis, such as in giant cell arteritis (GCA). Patients may have a history of preceding amaurosis fugax. Examination shows profound diminishment of visual acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and a pale fundus with preserved foveal color. CRAO is a medical emergency, as it an ischemic stroke of the ophthalmic vasculature and indicates a high risk for associated ischemic stroke to the brain. Patients who present with CRAO should be admitted to a stroke center for emergent evaluation, including a search for a possible embolic source with echocardiography and duplex ultrasonography of the carotid arteries. A careful history and laboratory evaluation of erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum concentration of C-reactive protein, and platelet count should be performed to evaluate for possible GCA. There is no proven medical or surgical therapy for CRAO, and the visual prognosis Is poor.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Acute angle-closure glaucoma (Choice A) typically presents with pain, conjunctiva! injection, a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, increased intraocular pressure, and no visible fundus abnormalities. If acute angle-closure glaucoma is not treated promptly it may result in profound, irreversible vision loss. Bacterial conjunctivitis (Choice B) presents with pain, conjunctiva ! injection, and purulent discharge.

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of facial numbness for 2 weeks. Her symptoms began as a "funny feeling" over a patch of skin on the left side of her chin and have gradual ly progressed to a 1 'novocaine" sensation. She has had no facial pain or numbness of the gums or oral mucosa. She has a 3-year history of breast cancer metastatic to the lungs treated with tamox ifen. Examination shows supraclavicular adenopathy. Sensation to pinprick, light touch, and temperature is absent over the left side of the chin. Neurologic examination shows no other abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely location of the abnormality?
correctExplanation: Numb chin syndrome, or mental neuropathy, is an indication of bony metastasis to the mandible in this patient with a history of breast cancer. The mandibular (V 3) branch of the trigeminal nerve passes through the bony canal of the mandible, branches to form the inferior alveolar nerve, and branches again proximal to the mental foramen to form the mental nerve. The mental nerve branch affected by mandibular bony metastases provides sensory innervation to the ipsilateral skin of the anterior chin (another unaffected mental nerve branch provides sensory innervation to the ipsilateral lower lip and buccal gingiva). Compression of the mental nerve branch by bony metastasis of the mandible leads to anesthesia of the chin. Numb chin syndrome may indicate systemic malignancy, autoimmune disease (eg, multiple sclerosis), or may be related to local infection, trauma, or dental disease. This patient should receive full-body imaging to evaluate for metastatic spread.

Classic symptoms include ipsilateral orbit pain, proptosis, periorbita l edema, and impairment in extraocular movement, pupil reactivity, or symmetry. questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman with AIDS comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of painful burning sensations in her hands and feet. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropr iate initial pharmacotherapy?

choices.E: Topical lidocaine to the affected areas

correctExplanation: Peripheral neuropathy is a frequent finding in patients with HIV and may occur either secondary to direct viral infection of peripheral nerves or secondary to neurotoxicity associated with antiretrovira l medications, frequent ly medications in the nucleoside analog reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) class. HIV-associated neuropathy most frequently presents with symmetric, distal polyneuropathy characterized by sensations of burning, tingling, or numbness in a stocking-g love distribution, as well as reduced vibratory or pinprick sensation. As with other forms of distal polyneuropathy, tricyclic antidepressants such as nortriptyline are effective as first-line treatment. Other effective treatments include gabapentin, pregabalin, lamotrigine, and topical capsaicin or lidocaine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Oral fluoxetine (Choice A) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and is not typically used as a first-line agent for peripheral neuropathic pain. While some SSRls, such as duloxetine, may be effective for the treatment of neuropathic pain, fluoxetine is not effective in treating nerve pain. Oral lorazepam (Choice B) is a short-acting benzodiazepine and is not recommended for the treatment of neuropathic pain because of its significant adverse effects and risk for dependency. Oral prednisone (Choice D) is a corticosteroid. While corticoste roids, including prednisone, may be effective for some forms of neuropathic pain, this is not an appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient given the significan t adverse effects of corticosteroid s, which includes immunosuppression. Topical lidocaine to the affected areas (Choice E) is not the best initial pharmacotherapy for peripheral neuropathy because they are less effective in comparison with systemic oral therapy such as tricyclic antidepressants. - - - - - - -- - - - .

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of moderate low back pain. He thinks he may have hurt his back while doing yard work. His pain moderate ly improves with rest; he has been spending a great amount of time in bed. He has not had other symptoms, weight loss, or a recent infection. He has no history of serious illness. His only medication is ibuprofen for the pain. He does not use intravenous drugs or anabolic steroids. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 102 kg (225 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. Examination shows mild paraspinal muscle tenderness. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Oxycodone therapy as needed for pain

correctExplanation: Low back pain is a common presenting complaint and it can be difficult to identify an exact underlying cause. Most nonspecific low back pain is attributed to muscu loskeletal injury from exertion, overuse, or trauma. The majority of these cases will resolve with conservative management, which includes activity modification, stretching, over-the-counter analgesics such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), massage, acupuncture, and heat therapy. Certain red flag signs and symptoms should prompt more urgent eva luation for a cause, especia lly if there is concern for infection, malignancy, or fracture. These include new fevers, intravenous drug use, focal neurologic deficits (such as urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bowel incontinence which may suggest cauda equina syndrome), progressive lower extremity neurologic symptoms, current or recent cancer history, advanced age, systemic corticosteroid use, and a significant traumatic mechanism. In this young, otherwise healthy patient with a mild inciting event, the next best step in management is continuation of ibuprofen therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bed rest for 10 days (Choice A) is not recommended for acute low back pain, as patients tend to have increased pain and a slower return to normal function. Activity modification for symptom relief should be advised, with encouragement to continue normal activities of daily living and non-exacerbating exertion. X-ray of the lumbar spine (Choice B) and MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice C) should be reserved for patients who present with red flag signs and symptoms to evaluate for evidence of fracture, infection, or malignancy. For otherwise healthy patients with back pain that has persisted for less than 4 weeks, imaging studies do not genera lly change management. Oxycodone therapy as needed for pain (Choice E) should be reserved for severe or refractory cases of acute low back pain.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 3 weeks after operative repair of a circle of Willis berry aneurysm. Her husband says that her behavior has changed since the operation. She is unmotivated and just sits around all day like a "bump on a log." She has not had depressed mood. Examination shows psychomotor retardation. She is oriented to person, place, and time. She is cooperat ive and her speech is fluent and grammatica l, but there is little spontaneous speech during conversation. Which of the following cerebral cortical regions is most likely affected?
correctExplanation: The patient is exhibiting symptoms of frontal lobe dysfunction. The frontal lobe is the largest lobe of the cerebra l cortex, separated from the parietal lobe by the central sulcus. The major areas of the frontal lobe are the primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, prefrontal cortex, Broca area, and the frontal eye fields. Symptoms depend on the location of the lesion. Involvement of the primary motor cortex and premotor cortex result in impaired motor function of the contralateral side of the body and psychomotor retardation. Disruption of Broca area may cause expressive aphasia with retention of language comprehension. Lesions of the frontal eye fields result in ipsilateral deviation of the eyes. Dysfunction of the prefrontal cortex can result in disinhibition, apathy, personality changes, aggressive behavior, and impairments in judgement, concentration, and orientation, as exhibited by this patient. Patients should be evaluated for other medical causes of cognitive impairment, such as vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) deficiency, hypothyroidism, syphilis infection, and intoxication. In this patient with a recent invasive procedure, CT scan or MRI of the brain is likely to show the diagnosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Insular (Choice B) cortex lesions may result in impairments in emotional and/or sensory processing, motor control, and speech. Patients may display a progressive expressive dysphasia characterized by non-fluent and grammatically incoherent speech. Occipital (Choice C) lobe lesions typically present with difficulties in processing visual sensory inputs. Patients may complain of visual field cuts depending on the precise location of the lesion. Parietal (Choice D) lobe lesions manifest differently depending on the side affected. Dominant parietal lobe lesions, most commonly on the left side, may result in Gerstmann syndrome, characterized by agraphia, aphasia, agnosia, acalculia, and right-left confusion. Nondominant parietal lobe lesions typically manifest with hemineglect of the contralateral side.

questionStem: A 10-day-old newbor n is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after a seizure that involved clonic jerking of the left arm. He had been well until 2 days ago when he began sleeping somewhat more but continued to feed well. Pregnancy, labor, and delivery were uncomplica ted. Vital signs are within normal limits. He is difficult to awaken but moves all extremities when stimulated. He is hypotonic but hyperreflexic. Babinski sign is present. During examinat ion, he has a clonic seizure of the right lower extrem ity. A CT scan of the head shows no abnorma lities. Cerebrospina l fluid analysis shows: Glucose Protein Leukocyte count Erythrocyte count A Gram stain is negative . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: 55 mg/dl 110 mg/dl 85/mm3 860/mm 3 Neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) encepha litis is the most likely diagnosis in this 10-day old infant with new onset seizures, a normal head CT scan, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showing increased protein and leukocyte count with a low-norma l glucose concentration, which is consistent with aseptic (nonbacteria l) meningitis. Further suggestive is the presence of erythrocytes in the CSF which is often seen in herpetic encepha litis. Most cases of HSV encephalitis are caused by HSV-2, although infection with HSV-1 occurs and is treated in the same way. Most patients acquire the virus via transmission from the mother, often during the third trimester, with encephalitis developing usually within a week. Symptoms are nonspecific and include fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and occasiona lly seizures or focal neurologic deficits. Concomitant oral lesions may occur, but their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. The CSF findings include increased protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and a normal or low-normal glucose concentration. In many instances the causative virus can be identified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the CSF, although empiric therapy with intravenous acyclovir is warranted prior to diagnosis. Failure to recognize and treat infection can result in organ dysfunction and death, or long-term neurologic sequelae.
incorrectExplanation: nd E.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician because of increasingly frequent headac hes during the past 3 months. The headac hes are throbbing, occur only on the right side, and are associated with nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. She has had one or two headaches yearly since the age of 17 years but now has two or three week ly. She is a schoolteacher and has had no changes in work, lifestyle, or environme nt. Four months ago, conjugated estrogen therapy was begun for treatment of menopausal symptoms. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Butalbital therapy combined with acetaminophen and caffeine

correctExplanation: Migraine is a common condition that presents with recurrent primary headaches. Migraine headaches are typically severe, unilateral, throbbing, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The pain is usually located behind or adjacent to the eye. Some patients additiona lly experience an aura before or during the headache, which may present with vision loss followed by the perception of scinti llating shapes or lines and/or paresthesia. Migraine triggers include stress, menstruation and changes in hormona l concen trations , weather changes, fasting, and alcohol. Sleep may improve migraines. Patients who experience migraines associated with conjugated estrogen therapy may require discontinuation of therapy or a reduction in dose. Migraines are postulated to arise from deficient serotonin inhibition of descending pain pathways. Acute migraine treatment may include triptans and/or nonsteroidal anti­ inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For patients with disabling or frequent migraines, prophylactic treatment is also recommended and includes ~-adrenergic blockers, antidepressants such as tricycl ic antidepressants and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and anticonvulsants.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. CT scan of the head (Choice A) is unnecessary given a likely cause for the patient's migraines and absence of any neurologic abnormalities. Butalbital therapy combined with acetaminophen and caffeine (Choice B) may be appropriate in the treatment of a primary migraine, however, it carries risk given the adverse effects and dependency associated with barbiturates. Removal of likely offending agents is a more appropriate first step for the treatment of this patient's likely-triggered migraine. - - - - .

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 1-month history of deafness, ringing in both ears, dizziness, and difficulty with balance. He also has had an occasiona l sensation that the room is spinning. He was discharged from the hospital 21 days ago after prolonged treatment for pneumon ia and sepsis with intravenous ceftriaxone and gentamicin. He has chronic obstruct ive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and congestive heart failure. He has a history of tubercu losis 10 years ago. Medications include digoxin, metformin, and losartan. His pulse is 84/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg. Examination shows nystagm us on lateral gaze bilatera lly. There is severe loss of hearing bilaterally. Air conduction is greater than bone conduct ion. Results of Weber test are normal. Muscle strength, deep tendon reflexes, and sensory findings are normal. His gait is broad-based, and he is unable to walk in tandem. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ototoxicity is a frequent adverse effect of aminoglycosides, such as gentamicin, which exert bactericidal effects by binding the bacterial 30S ribosoma l subunit. Aminoglycosides accumu late in the inner ear endolymph and perilymph, and can cause cochlear ototoxicity and vestibu lotoxicity, which is typically irreversible. The risk for ototoxicity associated with aminog lycosides may be as high as 10% in some patient populations. While there is an increased risk for ototoxicity with repeat dosing or with high doses, ototoxicity may occur with even the first dose of aminog lycoside. While aminoglycosides are high ly effective against a broad range of Gram-negative bacterial infections, such as with Escherichia coli, Klebsiel/a, Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Serratia species, their use is limited by their significant adverse effects. In addition to ototoxicity and vestibulotoxicity, aminoglycosides are also associated with nephrotoxicity.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cerebel lopontine angle tumor (Choice B), such as an acoustic neuroma, meningioma, or glioma, typical ly affects the vestibulococh lear nerve and other crania l nerves (eg, trigemina l, abducens, facial nerves). Patients may present with hearing loss and vertigo; sensory and motor dysfunction of the face and/or extraocular muscles are also possible. Meniere disease (Choice C) is a condition of episodic vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss that results from pressure accumu lation in the endolymph of the inner ear. This patient's lack of episodic symptoms suggests against this diagnosis. Pontine infarction (Choice D) may occur as a seque la of basilar artery occlusion and present with trunca l ataxia, diplopia, nystagmus, locked-in state, or coma.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of pain in the left thigh and flank and weakness of the left leg. She has a 30-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus currently controlled with glyburide. Examination shows weakness of the left iliopsoas and quadriceps muscles. Deep tendon reflex of the left quadriceps muscle is decreased. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the left latera l thigh and medial calf. Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion?
correctExplanation: Lower extremity neuropathies can be caused by nerve compression, ischemia, inflammation, degeneration, infection, or transection. Diabetic patients may develop spontaneous femora l neuropathies secondary to inflammation and ischemia. The femoral nerve arises from L2 to L4 and exits the lumbosacral plexus by passing under the inguinal ligament. Neuropathy of the femoral nerve or its roots presents with unilatera l quadriceps and iliopsoas weakness, decreased sensation over the anteromedial thigh and media l calf (the latter via its saphenous branch), and absent patellar tendon reflex.
incorrectExplanation: nd M. The axillary nerve (Choice A) arises from C5 and C6. Injury to the axillary nerve presents with weakness of shoulder abduction, as well as numbness over the deltoid region. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (Choice C) provides sensation to the antero latera l aspect of the thigh. The median nerve (Choice D) arises from C5 to T1. Injury to the median nerve causes weakness of the wrist flexors and muscles of the thenar eminence, and decreased sensation over the thenar eminence and the palmar aspect of the lateral 3½ fingers. The peronea l nerve (Choice E) is a continuation of the sciatic nerve that supplies innervation to the lateral leg. Injury causes weakness of muscles within the latera l compartment of the leg. A peroneal nerve lesion also causes numbness of the posterolateral side of the leg and the dorsolateral aspect of the foot.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of a progressive tremo r of his hands. He and his family have noticed that his movements have become more shaky during this period and that he has been walking more slowly during the past year. He has hypertension. Current medications include hydrochlorothiaz ide and aspirin. There is no family history of serious illness. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. His pulse is 56/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows a fine tremor of the hands at rest; the tremor is exacerbated with movement. There is cogwhee l rigidity of the upper extrem ities. His gait is slow and shuffling. Mental status examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Carbidopa-levodopa is a dopamine agonist used to treat Parkinson disease by increasing the amount of dopamine available in the nigrostriatal pathway. Carbidopa and levodopa are given together in order to increase availabi lity of levodopa to the brain. Levodopa is converted to dopamine by the enzyme dopa decarboxylase in the peripheral circulation and the brain. Dopamine is not able to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB), so any levodopa which is converted to dopamine peripherally is unable to effect change in the basal ganglia. Carbidopa indirectly increases dopamine availability in the basal ganglia by inhibiting dopa decarboxylase peripherally. In this way, more levodopa is able to cross the BBB and be converted to dopamine in the brain, where it is then able to act on the nigrostriatal pathway. Increased dopamine leads to improvement of Parkinson disease symptoms including the tremor, rigidity, akinesia, and postural instability shown by this patient.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Atenolol (Choice A), a ~-adrenergic blocker, and primidone (Choice E), a barbiturate, are both used in the treatment of essential tremor. This patient's resting tremor accompanied by unsteady gait and cogwhee l rigidity is more consistent with Parkinson disease. Donepezil (Choice C) is an anticholinesterase inhibitor which indirectly increases the concent ration of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. It is used to treat Alzheimer disease. Acetylcholine and dopamine have opposing effects in the basal ganglia related to movement such that decreasing acetylcholine has the same effect as increasing dopamine. Thus, medications which decrease, not increase, acetylcholine are used in Parkinson disease. Nifedipine (Choice D) is a calcium channe l blocker and does not play a role in the treatment of Parkinson disease.

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 2-hour history of a diffuse , bilateral, dull headac he. He has hypertens ion and has been poorly comp liant with his medicat ion. He is alert but confused. His blood pressure is 240/150 mm Hg. Funduscop ic examination shows hemo rrhages and exudates. Which of the following is the most likely d iagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy may result from acute and severe increases in blood pressure. It potentially manifests with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure, and may progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical dysfunction or from hypertensive retinopathy , including retina l hemorrhages and exudates. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops in blood pressure, which can cause end-organ ischemia. In general, a decrease in the mean arteria l pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correc tion over the next day or more following. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodilator and is a preferred agent because of its short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Cerebral hemorrhage (Choice A) can be idiopathic or secondary to trauma, aneurysms, arteriovenous malformations, tumors, or hypertension. Patients can present with a severe headache that can be associated with vomiting. In a patient with noncomp liance with antihypertensive medications, hypertensive encepha lopathy is more likely. Cerebral infarction (Choice B), or stroke , can occur as a sudden change in mental status as well as focal neurologic deficits and upper motoneuron signs. Patients typical ly present with acute focal neurologic deficits, especially on one side of the body, and may have speech difficulty, dysarthria, or aphasia. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice D) or pseudotumor cereb ri is an idiopathic increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) that typical ly occurs in obese women of childbearing age and presents with headaches that may be postural, visual deficits caused by pressure on the optic nerve, and nausea/vomiting (symptoms of increased ICP).

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of excessive sleepiness and fatigue. She has required more sleep for several years , but the problem has become increasingly worse during the past 7 months. She sometimes falls asleep in the middle of conversations and at dinner. She recently collapsed onto the floor of her apartment; she was aware o1f her surroundings but unable to move for 5 minutes. She has no history of seizures or other neurologic disorders. Her only medication is celecoxib for treatment of osteoarthritis. She appears well nourished. Physical examination shows limited range of motion in the lower extremities. There is swelling and crepitus of the knees. She has moderate pain on standing. An ECG, EEG, and 72-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring show no abnormalities. Polysomnography is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Methylphenidate is a non-amphetamine central nervous system stimulant medication that is used in the treatment of narcolepsy, which is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with fatigue and episodes of cataplexy. Methylphenidate works by blocking the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine into presynaptic neurons. The pathogenesis of narcolepsy involves the loss of orexin-A and orexin-B, which are neurotransmitters found primarily in the hypothalamus that promote wakefulness and inhibit rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Loss of these neurotransmitters permits abnormal transition from wakefulness to REM sleep with subsequent development of hallucinations and other features of narcolepsy including cataplexy and sleep paralysis. Diagnosis can be made in patients with daytime somnolence and cataplexy or, in cases where cataplexy is not present, with sleep latency testing. Polysomnography is appropriate to support the diagnosis and to rule out similar sleep-related conditions such as sleep apnea. Occasionally patients undergo lumbar puncture to directly measure concentrations of orexin-A in the cerebrospinal fluid, but this is generally not required for the diagnosis. Pharmacotherapy is directed at promoting wakefulness, and methylphenidate is one relatively safe and effective stimulant used to do this.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Mirtazapine (Choice B) is an antidepressant that increases presynaptic release of serotonin and norepinephrine. It tends to cause drowsiness and weight gain and is occasional ly used to treat patients with depression and sleep disturbances. Nortriptyline (Choice C) is a tricyclic antidepressant that is used to treat major depressive disorder and is used off label for a number of conditions including chronic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and diabetic neuropathy. It can cause drowsiness.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld right-ha nded woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of double vision and right-sided weakness that began while she was eating breakfast. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Medications include glyburide and atenolol. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min and regular, and blood pressure is 170/105 mm Hg. She is alert and oriented. Her speech is fluent but mildly slurred. She can follow complex commands. Cran ial nerve examination shows left ptosis. Adduction and elevation of the left eye are impai red. Ocular movements are full on the right. The right pupil is 3 mm, and the left pupil is 5 mm. The right pupil reacts normal ly, but the left pupil does not constrict either to direct or consensual light stimulation. There is drooping of the right side of the mouth. Muscle strength is normal in the left upper and lower extremities and is 4/5 in the right upper and lower extrem ities. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ on the right and 2+ on the left. Babinski sign is present on the right and absent on the left. There is no ataxia. Sensat ion is intact. Which of the following is the most likely location of this patient's lesion?
correctExplanation: This patient likely has a lesion of the left midbrain that affects the cerebral peduncle and the oculomotor nerve, which causes contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy, known as Weber syndrome. The cerebral peduncle refers to the anterior portion of the midbrain and includes the crus cerebri, which contains the corticospinal tract and is supplied by paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery. A brainstem lesion of the corticospinal tract leads to contralateral weakness in an upper motoneuron pattern of dysfunction (eg, spastic paralysis, Babinski sign, and hyperreflexia). The corticobulbar tract (located within the cerebral peduncle) may also be affected in Weber syndrome, leading to facial droop and weakness. The oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve Ill) is located anteriorly between the two cerebral peduncles and may be affected by strokes of the paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery, leading to ipsilateral dysfunction of the extraocu lar muscles and consequent diplopia, ptosis, and primary gaze palsy along with a deficit in pupillary constriction. Cerebral infarctions, or strokes, occur as a result of ischemic or hemorrhagic loss of blood supply to the brain. Risk factors for stroke include smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, carotid or intracranial atherosclerotic disease, history of hype rcoagu lability, atrial fibrillation, and advanced age. Classically, strokes manifest as a neurologic deficit related to the affected part of the brain.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Lesions of the left cerebral cortex (Choice A) may cause contralateral hemiparesis of the upper or lower extremities and facial weakness. However, oculomotor palsy would be atypical.

questionStem: Over the past 3 months, a 40-year-o ld woman has had multiple 1- to 2-minute episodes of numbness and tingling that begin in the right hand and then spread to the right arm and the face . Neurologic examination shows norma l findings. The most likely cause is a lesion at which of the following sites?
correctExplanation: Focal neurologic deficits that start in one area of the body and spread are suggestive of partial seizure activity. Without an alteration in level of consciousness, this would be defined as a simple partial seizure manifesting with sensory symptoms, also called a simple partia l somatosensory seizure. This type of seizure is most commonly associated with lesions of the parietal lobe as a result of the involvement of the primary somatosensory cortex, which processes sensory input from the contralatera l side of the body. Patients typica lly present with numbness, tingling, warmth, and/or pain. Other manifestations of parieta l lobe epileptic activity may include receptive aphasia, dyslexia, and other language/comp rehensio n disturbances because of involvement of Wernicke area at the junction of the parieta l and temporal lobes.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Frontal lobe (Choice A) lesions more commonly present with complex partial seizures, with impaired awareness as a result of the disruption of normal frontal lobe cognitive functions. Simple partial seizure activity with motor symptoms may also occur because of involvement of the primary motor cortex. Brainstem lesions involving the medulla (Choice B), midbrain (Choice C), or pons (Choice F) may result in foca l seizure activity characterized by convulsive movements; however, brainstem involvement more typically occurs with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Occipital lobe (Choice D) lesions are uncommon causes of focal seizure activity, but typically present with visual manifestations such as visual hallucinations, cortical blindness, and deviated gaze. ...

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 3-month histo ry of increasingly depressed mood, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and a decreased appetite resulting in a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss. He was diagnosed with Parkinson disease 2 years ago. He also has hypertension and benign prostatic hyperp lasia. His medications are amlodipine, carbidopa-levodopa, and tams ulosin. He has smoked one and one-half packs of cigarettes daily for 4 7 years. He states that he would like to stop smoking. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows mild cogwhee l rigidity, resting tremor of the hands, and gait instabi lity. On menta l status examination, he has a depressed mood and forlorn affect. Results of laboratory studies, including thyroid function tests, are within the reference ranges . Addition of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Bupropion can be utilized in patients with Parkinson disease, major depressive disorder, and nicotine use disorder to treat depression and promote abstinence from nicotine. Depression is a common complication of Parkinson disease. Since this patient's depression began after his Parkinson disease diagnosis, his depression is likely a result of Parkinson disease and should be diagnosed as depressive disorder caused by another medical condition. Many patients with this diagnosis improve once the medical condition resolves. Since Parkinson disease does not remit, the depression shou ld be treated pharmacologically. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line medications for patients with major depressive disorder and are frequent ly utilized for patients with comorbid Parkinson disease and major depressive disorder because of their effectiveness and low risk for adverse effects. However, serotonergic medications are not effective for smoking cessation. Bupropion is an antidepressant medication that increases the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine (which targets depressive symptoms) and antagonizes the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (which targets tobacco use). Bupropion can increase blood pressure, so this patient with a history of hypertension should have his blood pressure monitored closely.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Citalopram (Choice B) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, duloxetine (Choice C) is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, and mirtazapine (Choice E) is a selective a2-receptor antagonist and serotonin modu lator. All these medications can be utilized in major depressive disorder or depressive disorder caused by another medical condition (including Parkinson disease). However, none of these medications are effective for smoking cessation. - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - . -" .

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of visual hallucinations during the past 2 weeks. She has a 10-year history of hypertension and a 5-year history of Parkinson disease. Current medicat ions include hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, metopro lol, and carbidopa-levodo pa. Three weeks ago, her carbidopa- levodopa dose was increased because of decreased mobility, and metoprolo l was added to her medication regimen because of inadequate blood pressure contro l. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years but quit 10 years ago. She drinks one glass of wine with dinner every night. Her temperatu re is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 58/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 148/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Neurologic examination shows a resting tremor of the hands and cogwhee l rigidity. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the ankles. Her gait is shuffling. Mental status examination shows a constr icted affect. She is oriented to person but not to place or time. She can recall one of three objects after 5 minutes. She says she sees ghost-like figures entering the room. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. A CT scan of the head shows mild atrophy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's visual hallucinations?
correctExplanation: Adverse effect of carbidopa-levodopa is the most likely cause of this patient's visual hallucinations. Parkinson disease is a progressive neurologic disease that manifests with bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies, and a resting tremor. It is secondary to the destruction of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, so pharmacotherapy focuses on replacing dopamine with carbidopa-levodopa. Frequently, early in the disease course, treatment is effective, but over time, many patients experience an "on-off'' phenomenon whereby pharmacotherapy only works for a short time after each dose before the effects dissipate. This often prompts an increase in the dose of carbidopa-levodopa, or a change in the dosing interval, but in elderly patients this can result in multiple off-target adverse effects including hallucinations. This patient has no evidence of another underlying medical illness that may cause hallucinations, so the next step should be to lower the dose of carbidopa-levodopa to resolve her hallucinations. Patients who are intolerant or refractory to pharmacotherapy should be considered for deep brain stimulation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Major depressive disorder (Choice B) is diagnosed when patients meet criteria established in the DSM-5 including impaired sleep (either insomnia or hypersomnolence), loss of interest, guilt, loss of energy, poor concentration, poor appetite, psychomotor retardation , or suicidal ideation. This patient does not meet the criteria. \ j

questionStem: A 77-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of increasingly severe low back pain for 3 months. He has had poor control of bowel and bladder function for 2 weeks. He fell yesterday on his way to the bathroom . He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 60 years. Examination shows marked weakness of the lower extremities, normal upper extremity strength, bilateral brisk deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, a sensory level at T9, and a flaccid anal sphincter. There is tenderness over the lower thoracic spine. Babinski sign is present. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Epidural metastatic carcinoma resulting in spina l cord impingement is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with bowel and bladder incontinence, bilateral lower extremity weakness with hyperreflexia, and a sensory level at T9 that has developed over the preceding 3 weeks. Vertebra l masses may be the first presenting sign of a systemic malignancy, or they may be a late complication of metastatic disease. In either scenario, large masses can result in compression of the spina l cord at any segment, with subsequent sensory and motor deficits below the affected segment. In this instance, the sensory level at T9 likely indicates the presence of a mass at or just above the T9 vertebra l body in the epidura l space, with compression of the spinal cord at that level. Masses related to cancer must be distinguished from abscesses or hematomas, as the treatment between the entities differs significantly. Depending upon the type of cancer, steroids or radiation may be an initial option to reduce the inflammation associated with malignant compression of the spina l cord. In many cases, surgical decompression is required.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Carcinomatous meningitis (Choice A) can occur as a result of metastatic spread of a primary malignancy to the meninges around the brain, but it would present with headache and often with cranial nerve deficits. It does not present with neuro logic evidence of spinal cord dysfunction. Cervical spondylosis (Choice B) refers to gradual, age-related degenerative changes of the cervical spine with osteophyte development

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by his friend 30 minutes after being found unconscious in his bed. The patient lives alone in a trailer park, and his friend says he was well the night before. The patient has no history of serious illness and takes no medicat ions. He does not smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs. He appears well nourished. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. The nail beds and oral mucosa are pink. Neurolog ic examination shows no meningismus. The pupils are 4 mm and sluggishly reactive . The doll's eye (oculocephal ic) reflex is intact. There is no verbalization or eye opening in response to painful stimuli. He withdraws all extremities symmetri cally to painful stimuli. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ throug hout. Babinsk i sign is absent bilateral ly. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a Pco 2 of 30 mm Hg and Po 2 of 80 mm Hg. In addition to support ive care, which of the following is the most appropr iate therapy for this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning occurs as a consequence of inhaling the gas, often because of its generation in an area of poor ventilation (eg, a garage with door shut and car running, a space heater in a poorly-ventilated room, a malfunctioning basement furnace). CO is a byproduct of combustion. When inhaled, it avidly crosses the pulmonary capillary membrane and tightly binds hemoglobin, inducing a conformationa l change in the molecule and preventing the binding of oxygen. CO has an affinity for hemoglobin that is hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme. CO also has affinity with the mitochondrial electron transport chain, thus, in addition to hypoxemia resulting from interference with oxygen carrying capacity, cells may not be able to make use of the oxygen that they do receive via aerobic metabolism. As a result, anaerobic metabolism dominates, and lactic acidosis caused by hypoxia ensues. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, loss of consciousness, dizziness, vomiting, and fatigue; in severe cases, seizures, dysrhythmias, coma, and death may occur. Examination may show red skin. Treatment for CO poisoning begins with the administration of 100% oxygen regardless of pulse oximetry readings, and if any neurologic symptoms or signs of end-organ dysfunction are present, as in this case, hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Methylene blue (Choice B) is an antidote for methemoglobinemia; it serves to reduce iron in methemog lobin to Fe2+, restoring its ability to bind and transport oxygen. Methemoglobinemia may occur secondary to the use of nitrites and anesthetics.
