questionStem: A 5-year-o ld girl has the insidious onset of a clumsy gait over the past 3 months. Examination shows pes cavus of the left foot. There is generalized diminished girth of the left leg, and a decreased tendon reflex of the left ankle. The tendon reflexes at the knees are brisk. There is a sacral tuft of hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Tethered spinal cord, a defect in neural development whereby a caudal portion of the spinal cord becomes tethered to fixed fibrous structures that cause traction on the cord as the patient grows, is the most likely diagnosis. The filum terminale is a band of tissue that stretches between the caudal portion of the spinal cord and the sacrum, and persistent tethering of the spinal cord results in stretching as the child develops and axial growth occurs. Depending upon the severity, symptoms may present at infancy or can develop many years later, but progressive lower extremity neurologic dysfunction is typical as the spinal cord stretches and bends during normal activity. Sensory and gait abnormalities are typical, and bladder or bowel incontinence may also occur. Low back pain that worsens with activity and pain in the perineum can also occur. Clues to diagnosis include a tuft of hair over the sacrum or the presence of hemangiomas or dimples in the same region. Early detection and surgical intervention can improve symptoms and halt the progression of neurologic dysfunction.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Ataxia-telangiectasia (Choice A) is a genetic disorder that leads to early ataxia with progressively worsening gross and fine motor capabilities as children reach school age. Other findings include oculocutaneous telangiectasias and immunodeficiency. Friedreich ataxia (Choice B) is caused by a loss of function mutation in the frataxin gene resulting from a trinucleotide repeat. Patients usually present in adolescence with progressive ataxia of all limbs and dysarthria. Distal sensory loss and dysphagia may also be seen. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Choice C) has a diverse presentation but patients usually develop systemic symptoms including fevers and rash in addition to arthritis, which may affect nearly any joint. It does not present with asymmetric gait abnormalities or hyperreflexia. Spastic diplegia (Choice D) is a subtype of cerebral palsy and presents with symmetric spasticity of the lower extremities with associated sensory loss. In rare cases, the upper extremities may be involved, and intellectual disability can occur.

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman with AIDS comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressive right-sided weakness, slurred speech, and headache. She is right-handed. Funduscop ic examination shows papilledema . Neurologic examination shows aphasia, right homonymous hemianopia, and right-sided spastic weakness. A CT scan of the head with contrast shows multiple small ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema and mass effect in the left frontal, right occipital, and left parietal lobes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Toxop/asma gondii is an intracellular protozoan parasite. Transmission can occur through the ingestion of oocysts from cat feces or infected meat, direct transmission between a mother and fetus, or from organ transplantation, which leads to invasion followed by dissemination of the parasite where it typically lies dormant. It is a ubiquitous organism and nearly 10% of individua ls will be seropositive for T gondii, but the parasite does not usually cause severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. In patients with HIV infection and CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts less than 100 cells/mm 3, however, reactivation can occur with several distinct clinical syndromes of which cerebra l toxoplasmosis results in the most morbidity. Cerebral toxop lasmosis typical ly presents with multiple ring­ enhancing lesions scattered throughout the brain. Seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and systemic symptoms are common, as are signs of increased intracrania l pressure. Patients with HIV infection and positive Toxop/asma lgG antibodies are typically treated empirica lly with a sulfonamide and pyrimethamine if cerebra l toxoplasmosis is suspected, but confirmatory diagnosis occurs through a brain biopsy, which will show a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells, along with the presence of the T gondii organism. Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an AIDS-defining disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cryptococcosis (Choice A) is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, an encapsulated fungus and opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised patients. It can cause cryptococca l meningitis, encephalitis, and pulmonary cryptococcosis. Meningoencepha litis presents subacute ly with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, often accompanied by cough and shortness of breath caused by concurrent pulmonary infection. Focal neurologic deficits and mass lesions on neuroimaging are rare. Cysticercosis (Choice B) is caused by Taenia so/ium and presents with headache, seizures, and increased intracranial pressure. Neuroimaging will show cystic, ring-enhancing, calcified lesions in the brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, and/or orbit. It less commonly presents with focal neurologic deficits such as those seen in this patient.

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of progressive numbness and weakness of his legs. Six years ago, he had non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated successful ly with chemotherapy and radiation therapy. He is current ly taking no medications. Cranial nerve examination shows no abnormalities. Muscle strength is intact in the upper extremities but 3/5 in the proximal lower extremities and 4/5 in the distal lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the upper extremities and 3+ in the lower extrem ities. Babinski sign is present bilatera lly. Sensation to pinprick is decreased below the level of the nipples, and sensation to vibrat ion is decreased over the feet and ankles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Metastatic spinal cord compression occurs most commonly in prostate, lung, or breast cancer, although it can occur with any malignancy. It is generally caused by vertebral bony metastases that tend to occur in the vertebral body, particularly of the thoracic spine. Its presentation depends on the level of the lesion and the degree of spinal cord compression. Symptoms include back pain, which is often worse at night or with lying down, muscle weakness, sensory abnormalities, bladder or bowel dysfunction, and gait instability. It will general ly present with an upper motoneuron pattern of injury in the lower extremities with hyperreflexia and positive Babinski signs, as in this patient, assuming the compression is in the thoracic or upper lumbar region. Ascending numbness or paresthesias are also common. Diagnosis is classically made utilizing MRI of the spine. Patients may be treated with glucocorticoids, radiation therapy, and/or surgical decompression and spine stabilization.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chemotherapy-induced polyneuropathy (Choice A) classically presents with sensory loss and paresthesias in the distal extremities that ascend in a "stocking and glove" pattern. Most chemotherapy-induced polyneuropathy will improve over time after chemotherapy is stopped, making this a less likely explanation for this patient's acute onset of symptoms. Guillain-Barre syndrome (Choice B) is caused by autoimmune-mediated nerve destruction following a systemic infection, such as Campy/obacter jejuni. It classically presents with ascending paralysis with absent deep tendon reflexes that begins in the lower extremities. It can also ascend to involve the upper extremities, diaphragm, and crania l nerves in some patients. questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 62-year-o ld man has had progressive difficulty with speech and swallowing over the past year. Symptoms were subtle at first, and only he and his fam ily noticed a problem. Recent ly, two ham radio colleagues have commented that he sounds different on the air. He has also noticed that he has difficulty manipulating objects in the left hand, walking smooth ly, and going up and down stairs. He has not had any difficulty with his thought processes. Exami nation shows slow deliberate speech with mild dysarthria. Crania l nerves are otherwise norma l. There is wasting of intrinsic hand muscles and distal weakness in the left hand. Gait is slightly broad-based, but Romberg sign is absent. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in the left upper extremity, 2+ in the right upper extremity, and 3+ in the lower extremities. Jaw jerk is hyperactive . His serum potassium concentrat ion is 3.2 mEq/L. An x-ray of the chest shows normal findings. Wh ich of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.G: Epidural metastatic carc inoma P) Sensorimotor periphera l neuropa thy
choices.H: Epstein-Barr virus infectio n Q) Spinal cord compression

correctExplanation: Amyotrophic latera l sclerosis (ALS) is likely given insidious onset of upper and lower motoneuron deficits. ALS is caused by the progressive destruction of motoneurons. Patients may develop asymmetric weakness of the extremities. Unilateral hand weakness, foot drop, and bulbar symptoms (eg, dysphagia, voice changes) may occur simultaneous ly. On physica l examination, the presence of both upper motoneuron signs such as hyperreflexia and spasticity, combined with lower motoneuron signs such as hyporeflexia suggests the diagnosis. Parkinsonian features such as masked facies, tremor, and shuffling gait may occur, as can autonomic dysfunction. Eventually, patients deve lop respiratory insufficiency. The clinical progression is relent less and results in death.
incorrectExplanation: , M, N, 0, P, and Q. Alcoholic rhabdomyolysis (Choice A) refers to the breakdown of muscle and the release of creatine kinase in patients who consume large quantities of alcohol. Muscle pain and renal dysfunction may occur. Becker muscu lar dystrophy (Choice C) is a myopathy presenting with muscle weakness in the absence of upper motoneuron signs.

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld man is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-week history of difficulty with speech and weakness of his right leg. He has a 5-year history of HIV infection treated with antiretroviral therapy. On admiss ion, his temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows thrush. There is mild nonfluent aphasia. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the right lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in the right lower extrem ity and 2+ elsewhere. Babinski sign is present on the right. An MRI of the brain shows six ring-enhancing lesions in the cerebral hemispheres bilateral ly; the largest lesion is in the left frontal lobe. Some of the lesions have surroundi ng edema. Pyrimetham ine and sulfadiazine therapy is started. Two weeks later, there is no improvement in his symptoms. A second MRI of the brain shows no decrease in the size of the lesions, and some have increased in size. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma is a rare variant of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that occurs most commonly in immunocompromised patients. It can occur in the brain, spinal cord, leptomeninges, or eyes. Presenting symptoms include focal neurologic deficits, vision changes, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, headache, nausea, emesis). In immunocompetent patients, neuroimaging will most commonly show a solitary, hypodense periventricular mass with well­ defined borders and mild surrounding edema. In immunocompromised patients, however, the development of primary CNS lymphoma is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, with additional risk factors in HIV including a decreased CD4+ T lymphocyte count, increased viral load, and chronic co-infection with hepatitis B or C virus. Imaging in immunocompromised patients more commonly shows multifocal disease, numerous, ring- or heterogeneously enhancing lesions throughout the corpus callosum, periventricular areas, and periependyma l regions. The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow cytometry or cytology, with evidence of EBV DNA in the CSF supporting the diagnosis. Treatment typically consists of high-dose and generally intrathecal chemotherapeutics and antiretroviral therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Candida! abscesses (Choice A) of the brain can occur in immunocompromised patients. These are typically microabscesses that can lead to the development of encepha lopathy with altered mental status and are seen on MRI as small, ring-enhancing lesions often with a hemorrhagic component. However, these patients commonly present with fever, nuchal rigidity, and headache, which this patient does not demonstrate.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes fo r a routine health maintenance examination. She is concerned about developing dementia because she lives alone; she does not want to be a burden to her children. Her father was just diagnosed with dementia, Alzheimer type. She takes no medicat ions other than hydroch lorothiazide for hypertension. Her blood pressure is 124/84 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following measures is most likely to decrease her risk for multi-infarct (vascular) dementia?

choices.E: Daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation

correctExplanation: Vascular dementia is the second most common form of dementia after Alzheimer type, characterized by stepwise cognitive decline following recurrent cerebral infarctions (strokes). The rate of decline and specific symptoms depend on the regions of the brain affected, and patients typically develop cognitive impairment, motor dysfunction, and behavioral changes as the disease progresses. Risk factors include age, hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and prior cerebrovascular accidents. Diagnosis is made clinically with support of neuroimaging demonstrating cerebral ischemic changes. Risk factor reduction is the primary approach to prevention. Continued control of blood pressure is most likely to decrease the risk for this patient developing vascular dementia.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Efforts to reduce overall cardiovascular risk factors should be encouraged, which includes regular aerobic exercise (Choice B). Daily fish oil supplementation (Choice D) and daily vitamin E supplementation (Choice F) have also been shown to have a mild protective effect. However, control of blood pressure has a stronger association with cardiovascular risk reduction. Daily aspirin prophylaxis (Choice C) is recommended for patients who have existing clinically significant cardiovascular disease (such as history of a myocardial infarction or cerebrovascular event). It is not likely to significantly lower the risk for vascular dementia in this patient. Daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation (Choice E) is recommended for women who are postmenopausal, patients taking chronic systemic corticosteroids, and patients with advanced renal disease to reduce the risk for osteoporosis and fragility fractures. questionStem: A previous ly healthy 45-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after she lost consciousness while shopping in a department store; on regaining consciousness, she had a severe headache and photophobia. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examinat ion shows slight neck stiffness with flexion. There is pain with lateral deviation of the eyes. Neurologic examinat ion shows no other abnormalities. A CT scan of the head shows no lesions or evidence of bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Discharg ing the patient with analgesic therapy

correctExplanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) refers to bleeding into the subarachnoid space and can be caused by aneurysmal or non-aneurysma l rupture of an artery in the subarachnoid space. Patients typically present with an acute, severe headache (often described as the worst headache of their life), along with neck stiffness, photophobia, and possible stupor or coma in severe cases. Fever can be associated with SAH and is associated with worse outcomes. CT scan of the head typically shows hyperdense blood products in the cerebral sulci and basal cisterns. However, the sensitivity of CT scan for SAH is lower with small volume bleeding or a delayed presentation. If there is strong suspicion for SAH with a negative CT scan, a lumbar puncture can be performed, which may show red blood cells or xanthochromia, which represents hemoglobin degradation products. As the blood products circulate within the subarachnoid space, complications include the development of communicating and/or obstructive hydrocephalus in the acute stage, along with the potential for re-bleeding and vasospasm in the days following the initial bleed. It is a neurosurgical emergency that may be fatal if progressive or untreated.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Admission for observation (Choice A) would not be indicated until further workup is performed to evaluate for subarachnoid hemorrhage. First, a subarachnoid hemorrhage should be investigated by lumbar puncture, and if findings are consistent with subarachnoid hemorrhage, vessel imaging should occur to evaluate for aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Discharging the patient with analgesic therapy (Choice B) would be dangerous in the care of this patient, as further evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage is indicated. The patient is at risk for hydrocephalus, vasospasm, rebleeding, or severe hemorrhage after a sentinel bleed.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after the onset of double vision, loss of balance , and dizziness. She has no history of similar symptoms. She sustained a myocardial infarctio n 2 months ago. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include insulin and clonidine. She appears anxious. Her temperatu re is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg in both arms. A left carotid bruit is heard. Pulses are decreased in the lower extremities. Atherosclerotic involvement of which of the following arteries is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: This patient likely has an occlusion of the vertebral artery leading to vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Vertebrobasilar insufficiency can be caused by ischemia in patients with poor sympathetic regulation or thromboembolism commonly originating from an atherosclerotic plaque in or dissection of a vertebral artery (known as a posterior circulation stroke). Risk factors for posterior circulation strokes include smoking, hypertension, age, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and peripheral artery disease (as evidenced by this patient's diminished lower extremity pulses). The brain stem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes are commonly affected. Patients typically present with vestibulocerebel lar signs (eg, ataxia, dysmetria, dizziness, imbalance, vertigo, vomiting, nystagmus), ipsilateral cranial nerve dysfunction (eg, dysphagia, dysarthria, vertical or horizontal gaze palsies), contralatera l hemipa resis (caused by corticospinal tract damage), contralateral impairment in pain and temperature sensation (caused by spinothalamic tract damage), and/or contralateral homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing (caused by posterior cerebral artery involvement). Unlike hemisphe ric strokes arising from the internal carotid arteries, cortical deficits such as cognitive and speech impairment are typically absent. A noncontrast CT scan of the head rules out hemorrhage, and the diagnosis may be confirmed with vessel imaging if the lesion is sufficiently large. If no hemorrhage is seen, acute management of posterior circulation strokes may involve tissue plasminogen activator therapy or thrombectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. The brachiocephalic artery (Choice A) supplies the arm, head, and neck. Atherosclerotic disease and consequent occlusion of the brachiocephalic artery may lead to neck and upper extremity pain in addition to signs of vertebrobasilar insufficiency that are exacerbated on exercise.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman with alcoholism is hospitalized for detoxification. On the second day after admission, she has an impaired sensor ium and a decreased attention span during examination. She appears frightened and disoriented and shrieks, "Make the snakes go away." Her temperatu re is 38.3°C (101 °F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 190/120 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: This patient has developed delirium tremens, a serious complication of alcoho l withdrawal. Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol results in imbalanced and unopposed sympathetic excess. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can begin within hours after the cessation of alcohol use. Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, involves severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visua l hallucinations, and autonomic instability (generally characterized by tachycardia, hypertension, and potentially hyperthermia). As in this patient, delirium tremens can begin 2 to 5 days after the patient's last alcoho lic drink. Delirium tremens is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (GABA A receptor agonists) to address the psychomotor agitation associated with withdrawal and prevent the worsening of withdrawa l manifestations. The specific benzodiazepines utilized include chlordiazepoxide, a long-acting benzodiazepine given on a scheduled basis in patients experiencing or at risk for complicated withdrawal (eg, delirium tremens), and/or lorazepam, a short-acting benzodiazepine given as-needed for withdrawal symptoms. Management also includes frequent assessments including vital sign checks, fluid resuscitation, and nutritiona l supplementation (especial ly with commonly deficient vitamins and minerals such as thiamine, potassium, and magnesium).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. CT scan of the head (Choice A) and oral thioridazine (Choice C), a first-generation antipsychotic, would be unnecessary in this patient whose acute-onset disorientation and hallucinations are consistent with delirium tremens. Psychosis and agitation related to alcohol withdrawal should be treated with benzodiazepines rather than antipsychotics. Intravenous antibiotic therapy (Choice D) would be unnecessary in this patient whose hyperthermia and tachycardia are consistent with delirium tremens rather than infection.

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe low back pain and severe shooting pain down her left buttock and leg. The pain began when she arose quickly from a seated position to open a sliding glass door. Two analgesic tablets leftover from a dental procedure provided no relief. She is an avid cyclist. On arrival, intravenous administration of morphine is begun and provides minimal relief. The patient notes numbness over the perineum when she attempts to void. She is reluctant to move from a flexed, seated position to a stretcher because of the pain. Muscle strength is 3/5 on great toe extension, dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion of the left foot. Knee jerk is present on the left. Achilles tendon reflex is absent on the left. An MRI of the lumbosacra l spine shows a large central herniation at L4-5 that compresses the L5 and S1 nerves on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome occurs as a result of compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs because of malignancy, trauma (eg, compression fractures with fragment retropulsion), disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal epidura l or subdural hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by inability to void and urinary retention. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression. Initial treatment for patients with epidural spinal cord compression and neurologic deficits include symptomatic treatment, pain control, and glucocorticoid therapy prior to operative therapy. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy is helpful as a bridge to definitive therapy , can help control pain, and may transiently improve neurologic function secondary to decreasing edema at the site of cord compression. However, cauda equina syndrome is a surgica l emergency and requires decompression with lumbar laminectomy as soon as possible.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. A bone scan (Choice A) is used to examine and diagnose abnormalities in bones, such as bony metastases, fractures, or osteomyelitis. It is not used to evaluate neuromuscular weakness. Physical therapy (Choice B) can be used in the management of other types of back pain, such as lumbosacral strain. However, lumbosacra l strain will not cause perinea! anesthesia or neuromuscular weakness. Cauda equina is a surgical emergency, making physical therapy an incorrect initial next step.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld man comes to the physician 2 hours after the onset of dizz iness, nausea, and unsteadi ness . He had a whiplash neck inju ry 2 years ago and is still receiving monthly chiropractic man ipulations. His voice is hoarse . There is left ptosis and nystagmus . The left pupil is 2 mm smaller than the right. There is decreased sensation to pain over the left side of the face and right extrem ities. He has atax ia on the left. Mental status exam ination shows no abnorma lities. Wh ich of the following arteries is most likely to be occluded?

choices.F: Left posterior cerebral M) Right vertebra l

correctExplanation: This patient likely has an occlusion of the left vertebra l artery leading to vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Vertebrobasi lar insufficiency can be caused by ischemia in patients with poor sympathetic regulation or thromboembolism common ly originating from an atherosclerotic plaque in or dissection of the vertebra l artery (known as a posterior circulation stroke). A thrombus of the vertebral artery commonly forms from atherosclerotic disease but may also form as a result of an intima l defect from trauma or vertebra l artery dissection, a known complication of chiropractic manipu lation. The brain stem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes are common ly affected. Patients typica lly present with vestibu locerebe llar signs (eg, ataxia, dysmetria, dizziness, imbalance, vertigo, vomiting, nystagmus), ipsilatera l cranial nerve dysfunction (eg, dysphagia, dysarthria, vertical or horizonta l gaze palsies), contralateral hemiparesis (caused by corticospinal tract damage), contralateral impairment in pain and temperature sensation (caused by spinothalamic tract damage), and/or contra latera l homonymous hemianopsia with macu lar sparing (caused by posterior cerebral artery involvement). In posterior circulation strokes affecting the lateral pons, Horner syndrome may occur, which presents with unilateral ptosis and miosis (pupil lary constriction) and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis. If no hemorrhage is shown on noncontrast CT scan of the head, acute management of posterior circu lation strokes may involve tissue plasminogen activator therapy or thrombectomy. In dissection, antiplatelet and anticoagu lant administration is indicated to prevent conversion to a thromboembolic stroke if none has yet occurred.
incorrectExplanation: nd M. The basilar artery (Choice A) is supp lied by the vertebra l arteries. Compared to vertebral artery occlusion, basilar artery occlusion may present with more acute and severe corticospina l and corticobu lbar dysfunction, leading to locked-in syndrome. The vertebral arteries are more vulnerable than the basilar artery to chiropractic manipu lation-related intimal injury.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician because of a 4-month history of headac hes and blurred vision. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medicat ions. Menses occur at irregular 2- to 10-week intervals . She has had an 18-kg (40-lb) weight gain during the past 7 months. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and now weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Her tem perature is 37°C (98.6 °F). Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Visua l field testing shows no abnorma lities. Funduscop ic examination shows blurred optic discs; there are no spontaneous venous pulsations. The rema inder of the exam ination shows no abnormalities. A CT scan of the head shows small lateral ventricles. On lumbar puncture, the opening pressure is 290 mm H 20; cerebrospina l fluid (CSF) analysis shows no leukocytes or erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
correctExplanation: Impaired resorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is the primary mechanism behind pseudotumor cerebri, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). IIH is characterized by signs of increased intracranial pressure including headache, papilledema, and increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture without any underlying pathology to cause such findings on neuroimaging. It is primari ly seen in young women who are overweight. Although there is no malignant cause underlying the increased intracranial pressure, it may cause debilitating headaches and permanent vision loss. Headaches that are secondary to increased intracranial pressure often are worse when lying down and relieved by standing. The most common risk factors for the development of pseudotumor cerebri include female gender and obesity. However, hypervitaminosis A from increased dietary intake is another potentia l cause of IIH. This can be from excessive dietary intake or from the use of retinoid medications such as isotretinoin or all-trans retinoic acid. Other medications associated with IIH include tetracyclines, danazo l, and growth hormone.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aqueductal stenosis (Choice A) causes dilation of the lateral and third ventricles and is a cause of hydrocephalus in children. Idiopathic increased intracranial pressure presents with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (nausea, vomiting, positiona l headache) without hydrocepha lus. Cerebel lar astrocytoma (Choice B) is a primary centra l nervous system tumor seen most often in children and a potential cause of secondary intracranial hypertension and hydrocepha lus if it obstructs the flow of CSF. IIH is characterized by increased intracranial pressure but not hydrocephalus.

questionStem: A 6-year-o ld boy is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after a motor vehicle collision in which he was the unrestra ined front seat passenger; he lost consciousness momentarily. Exami nation shows a 2 x 2-cm area of soft-tissue swelling over the forehead, a small abrasion on the left cheek, and an abras ion on the right elbow. Neurologic findings are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Mild traumat ic brain injury, also known as a concussion, commonly results in the loss of consciousness, confusion, amnesia, headache, dizziness, nausea, and/or vomiting minutes after the injury. A concussion can be caused by direct or indirect blunt head trauma and typica lly causes self-limited brief neurologic impairment , such as the loss of consciousness, repetitive questioning, or confusion. Symptoms that commonly develop within the following days include mood disturbances, photophonophobia, trouble concentrating, and/or insomnia. Patients do not have focal neurologic symptoms such as limb weakness or vision changes that would indicate traumatic vascular injury or intracran ial hemorr hage. All patients with suspected concussion should undergo a thorough neurologic examination, and a subset of at-risk patients should receive neuro imagi ng. All patients should be monitored close ly for neurologic deterioration, which may indicate a deve loping intracran ial hem1atoma. To prevent cumulative brain injury (eg, from a second concussion), patients with concussion shou ld return to their usual activities in a graded fashion, beginning with the return to schoo l and without return to sports until cleared by a physician. questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 6-month-o ld girl is brought to the emergency depa rtment by ambulance because of difficulty breathing. Her mothe r says that she fell from the couch to a carpeted floor yesterday. She cried immedia tely and was fine until several hours later when she could not be aroused and seemed to be gasping for breath . Her mother noticed some emesis in the bed. On arrival , she is letha rgic. Her tempera ture is 36.5 °C(97.7 °F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg. Exami nation shows a bulging anterior fontanelle. There are bilateral retinal hemo rrhages. Neurologic examination shows no foca l findings . A CT scan of the head shows blood along the falx. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.F: Diffuse axona l injury M) Skull fractu re over the middle meningea l artery

correctExplanation: Severe intracranial injury with a history inconsistent with the severity of the patient's physical findings raises suspicion for abusive head trauma and non-accidental trauma. Patients with abusive head trauma can present with encepha lopathy, apnea, seizures, and retinal hemorrhages. The mechanism of abusive head trauma is typica lly blunt force or shaking, which results in an acceleration-deceleration force on the infant. Infants are vulnerable to dece leration injury because of several factors. The large head and weak neck muscu lature result in greater movement of the brain in the intracrania l space when acted upon by acceleration and deceleration force such as in shaking. In addition, the infant skull is thin, allowing forces to transfer through the skull to the brain. Findings on CT scan associated with non-accidental head trauma include subdural hemorrhage, especial ly multiple hemorrhages or those in an interhemispheric or posterior fossa location, hypoxic-ischemic injury, and cerebral edema.
incorrectExplanation: , M, and N. Basilar skull fractures (Choice A) typica lly occur after high-impact blunt head injury and wou ld be unlikely in this patient. Patients can present with hemotympanum, detected RBC in analysis of cerebrospina l fluid, bloody otorrhea or rhinorrhea, mastoid and periorbital ecchymosis, and crania l nerve palsy. Caput succedaneum (Choice B) refers to extraperiostea l swelling or ecchymosis on a neonate's scalp with poorly defined margins following vaginal delivery. It is a common and benign condition that reso lves spontaneously.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a ?-month history of progressive bilateral leg pain. She describes bilateral buttock, posterior thigh, and calf pain that begins after standing or walking for 10 minutes. It is relieved in 2 minutes by bending forward at the waist or sitting. She has coronary artery disease and underwent coronary artery bypass grafting 2 years ago. Neurologic examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Doppler flow studies of the lower extremities

correctExplanation: The patient is presenting with symptoms suggestive of spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. Spinal stenosis describes narrowing of the central canal, neural foramen, or lateral recesses of the spine with subsequent nerve compression and ischemia. Common causes include degenerative arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, degenerative disc disease, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, and osteophyte formation in the facet joints. Neurogenic claudication describes low back pain with radiation to the buttocks and lower extremities that results from increased nerve compression, as may occur with extension of the spine during standing and walking downhill. Reducing narrowing within the spinal column with spinal flexion as during sitting or walking uphill tends to relieve the pain. Diagnostic evaluation involves x-ray imaging followed by MRI of the lumbar spine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Carotid duplex ultrasonography (Choice A) is recommended to screen for atherosclerotic plaque in patients with a known cardiovascular disease history or significant risk factors. If a stroke or transient ischemic attack were suspected as the cause of the patient's neurologic symptoms, carotid duplex ultrasonography should be performed to evaluate for intervenab le lesions. The exacerbating and alleviating factors in this case are more suggestive of spinal stenosis. Doppler flow studies of the lower extremities (Choice B) are useful in distinguishing neurogenic claudication from claudication caused by peripheral vascu lar disease. Vascular claudication is typically relieved by rest as opposed to postura l changes. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies (Choice C) can be used to confirm the presence of radiculopathy caused by nerve root compression or evaluate for other myopathy or neuropathy as the cause of the patient's symptoms. These tests are reasonable if the diagnosis is still in doubt after the initial imaging studies. MRI is the most appropriate next step.

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman has had throbbing right-sided headac hes that began gradua lly 6 weeks ago and have increased in frequency and severity. The headac hes typ ically begin in the morning short ly after arising, last up to 1 hour, and occur several times daily. Acetaminophen has prov ided partia l relief. She is irritable and has been unable to keep up daily activities. She appears upset. Neurolog ic examination shows a persistent attention deficit and left arm drift. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?

choices.C: Cerebra l nerve root impingeme nt

correctExplanation: This patient's examination findings of attention deficit (likely neglect) and left arm drift are suggestive of the presence of a contra lateral upper motoneuron lesion, which, in conjunction with her symptoms of new chronic headache, is suggestive of a brain tumor. Hemispatia l neglect often occurs as a result of lesions of the parietal cortex and may also occur in stroke. Simi larly, left arm drift may be suggestive of an upper motoneuron lesion in a variety of locations, such as the contra latera l frontal cortex, cerebe llum, or pyramida l tract. Collective ly, this patient's findings localize her lesion to the right parietal cortex.
incorrectExplanation: Cerebral hemorrhage (Choice B) may present with abrupt and acute onset of headache and focal weakness or numbness. Cerebral nerve root impingement (Choice C) may cause radiculopathy and present with weakness, numbness, paresthesia, and pain in the dermatomal and myotomal distribution that correlates to the affected root. Cluster headache (Choice D) is a primary headache that typical ly presents with short-lived, unilatera l, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbita l, or tempora l region of the head and is accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, miosis, ptosis, lacrimation, nasal congestion). Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice E) presents commonly in younger, overweight females taking vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazo l. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision. questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of increasingly severe pain, swelling, and numbness of her left arm and shoulder; during the past 8 weeks, she has had difficulty moving her left arm because of these symptoms. Fifteen years ago, she underwent a left radical mastectomy followed by radiation therapy of the chest wall for breast cancer. There has been no evidence of recurrence of breast cancer. She has hypertension treated with atenolol. Her only other medication is ibuprofen as needed for pain. Her tempera ture is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows no neck, axillary, or chest wall masses. There is 2+ pitting edema of the entire left upper extremity. Examination of the right upper extremity shows no abnorma lities. Radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ and equal bilaterally. Sensat ion to pinprick and motor function of the left upper extremity are absent. A photograph of the chest wall and left upper extremity is shown. An MRI of the left upper extrem ity and shoulder shows fibrosis but no masses. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

correctExplanation: Radiation-induced brachia ! plexopathy is a potential complication of radiation to the brachia ! plexus, most common ly occurring after radiation therapy for breast or lung cancer. Radiation damages the brachia! plexus and presents with symptoms of brachia ! neuritis, including pain, paresthesia, and weakness in the distribution of the affected nerves that may occur months or years after the initial insult. In this scenario, the radiation has likely affected the C5 and C6 nerve roots (called Erb Palsy), leading to dysfunction of the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps brachii muscles, resulting in impaired upper extremity abduction, lateral rotation, flexion, and supination. Consequent ly, the patient's upper extremity hangs near the body in a medially rotated, extended, and pronated position as shown in the photograph. questionStem: An 82-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he collapsed while walking in his garden. He has hypercholesterolemia. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 60 years. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. He is awake but is unable to speak due to facial and tongue paralysis. He is able to blink his eyes and move his eyes vertically on command. He cannot move his eyes laterally. Examination shows complete paralysis of all extrem ities. Sensation to touch is intact. He undergoes endotracheal intubation for airway protection, and intravenous hydration is begun. An MRI of the brain shows extensive infarction of the base of the pons due to basilar artery occlusion. Conservative treatment is recommended . Although he cannot speak, he can commun icate clearly by means of a code using eye blinks. The patient clearly commun icates to his physicians repeatedly that he wants no life support or artificia l hydration, and wants to die because of his poor prognosis for recovery. His wife and two sons agree with this decision but an estranged daughter does not and is threatening legal action. Which of the following is the most appropr iate next step in management?

choices.A: A court order must be obtained to determine what life-sustaining measures, if any, may be withdrawn
choices.B: An ethics team consultation should be obtained and their decision followed concerning what life support measures, if any, may be

correctExplanation: Neurologically impaired patients should not be assumed to lack decisiona l capacity to make decisions about their care. The medical team should evaluate the decisiona l capacity of this patient who is making decisions about his end-of-life care. This patient is able to communicate a consistent decision and demonstrate an appreciation of the consequences of his decision, and therefore, he appears to possess decisiona l capacity to make the decision to withdraw care. The medica l team should respect the patient's autonomy and withdraw care. If a patient lacks decisional capacity, the medical team should identify a surrogate decision-maker. Unless the patient has identified a durable power of attorney, the spouse should serve as decision maker (adult children are typica lly second in line, followed by parents). Further reassuring in this case is that the patient's wife and adult children corroborate his decision.
